Senadores e deputados federais, estaduais e distritais são definidos no primeiro turno e não disputam segundo turno.

articles.title: Quem vai às urnas neste domingo? Veja o perfil dos eleitores brasileiros em 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Brasil tem 158,7 milhões de pessoas aptas a votar. Levantamento mostra o perfil do eleitorado por idade, gênero, estado e autodeclaração de raça ou cor.
articles.summary: Brasil tem 158,7 milhões de pessoas aptas a votar. Levantamento mostra o perfil do eleitorado por idade, gênero, estado e autodeclaração de raça ou cor.
articles.body:
As mulheres representam a maioria do eleitorado brasileiro, e quase um em cada quatro eleitores tem 60 anos ou mais. Esse é o perfil dos 158,7 milhões de brasileiros aptos a votar neste domingo (4), no primeiro turno das eleições de 2026. Os números são do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE).

Os brasileiros vão votar para presidente, governador, senador (duas vagas por estado), deputado federal e deputado estadual ou distrital, no caso do Distrito Federal.

Do total de pessoas aptas a votar, 157,8 milhões estão registradas no Brasil e 918,9 mil, no exterior. Quem tem domicílio eleitoral fora do país vota apenas para presidente da República.

Mulheres são 52,84% do eleitorado, com 83,9 milhões de eleitoras.

Pessoas com 60 anos ou mais somam 37,5 milhões, ou 23,6% do total.

Jovens de 16 e 17 anos representam 1,03% dos eleitores, com 1,6 milhão de registros.

São Paulo, Minas Gerais e Rio de Janeiro concentram 63,3 milhões de eleitores.

Quase 2 milhões de pessoas têm deficiência registrada no cadastro eleitoral.

Mulher vota na urna eleitoral em cabina de votação — Foto: Roberto Jayme/Ascom/TSE

O eleitorado feminino reúne 83.877.126 pessoas, o equivalente a 52,84% do total. Os homens somam 74.845.001, ou 47,15%.

A diferença é de cerca de 9 milhões de eleitoras a mais. Outros 23.336 registros não têm informação de gênero.

Idoso de 82 anos vota para 'conviver com a própria consciência' — Foto: Gyovanna Soares/g1

Os brasileiros com 60 anos ou mais somam 37.457.537 eleitores e representam 23,6% das pessoas aptas a votar.

Consideradas separadamente as faixas etárias do cadastro, o maior grupo é o de 40 a 44 anos, com quase 16 milhões de pessoas, 10,08% do eleitorado.

Veja as cinco faixas com mais eleitores:

Somadas, as faixas de 30 a 59 anos concentram 87,1 milhões de pessoas, ou 54,85% do eleitorado.

A menos de um ano da eleição, TSE incentiva jovens a tirar título de eleitor — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

O país tem 1.634.244 eleitores de 16 e 17 anos, faixa em que o voto é facultativo. São 606.603 com 16 anos e 1.027.641 com 17 anos.

Juntos, eles representam 1,03% do eleitorado.

Além dos adolescentes dessas idades, pessoas analfabetas e aquelas a partir dos 70 anos também podem escolher se vão votar, sem obrigação de comparecer.

No cadastro do TSE, 22,2 milhões de eleitores estão classificados na categoria de voto facultativo, o equivalente a 13,99% do total. Para os outros 136,5 milhões, o voto é obrigatório.

São Paulo concentra mais de um quinto dos eleitores

Eleitores comparecem para votação no segundo turno das eleições de 2024 em São Paulo — Foto: Paulo Pinto/Agência Brasil

São Paulo é o maior colégio eleitoral do país, com 34.104.226 pessoas aptas a votar. O estado concentra 21,48% do eleitorado brasileiro, incluindo os registros no exterior.

Na sequência, aparecem Minas Gerais, com 16,4 milhões, e Rio de Janeiro, com 12,9 milhões. Juntos, os três estados reúnem 63,3 milhões de eleitores, 39,9% do total.

Veja os cinco maiores colégios eleitorais:

Na outra ponta, Roraima tem o menor eleitorado entre os estados: 401.496 pessoas. Depois aparecem Amapá, com 577.534, e Acre, com 614.375.

Quase 2 milhões têm deficiência registrada

Eleitores com deficiência ou mobilidade reduzida podem solicitar serviço de transporte gratuito ao TRE-AM. Prazo para solicitação vai até o dia 14 de setembro. — Foto: Júnior Souza/TRE-AM

O cadastro eleitoral reúne 1.970.165 pessoas com deficiência informada, o equivalente a 1,24% do eleitorado.

Há também 38.472 eleitores com nome social registrado.

Já a biometria está cadastrada para 141.301.540 pessoas, ou 89,01% dos eleitores, aproximadamente nove em cada dez.

Maioria dos cadastros não informa raça ou cor

A informação de raça ou cor não está preenchida em 126 milhões de registros, o equivalente a 79,38% do eleitorado.

Por isso, os dados disponíveis não permitem descrever a composição racial de todos os brasileiros aptos a votar.

Entre os registros com autodeclaração, os números são:

Os pardos formam o maior grupo entre quem tem raça ou cor informada. Isso não significa, porém, que representem a maioria de todo o eleitorado, já que a informação está ausente em quase oito de cada dez cadastros.

Cadastro reúne 287 mil eleitores autodeclarados indígenas

O levantamento registra 287.157 eleitores que se autodeclararam indígenas no campo de raça ou cor.

O Amazonas concentra o maior contingente, com 73.580 registros. Depois aparecem Pernambuco, com 28.384; Roraima, com 22.165; Mato Grosso, com 21.459; e Mato Grosso do Sul, com 17.234.

No arquivo que detalha o pertencimento a grupos indígenas, os maiores contingentes identificados são Tikúna, com 19.062 eleitores; Makuxí, com 14.935; e Kokama, com 12.551.

articles.title: Candidatos à Presidência votam acompanhados de aliados e familiares | G1
articles.standfirst: Lula, Flávio, Cury, Caiado, Zema e Renan votaram pela manhã e acompanham a apuração dos votos ao longo do dia em seus estados.
articles.summary: Lula, Flávio, Cury, Caiado, Zema e Renan votaram pela manhã e acompanham a apuração dos votos ao longo do dia em seus estados.
articles.body:
Montagem com fotos dos candidatos à Presidência: Lula (PT), Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Augusto Cury (Avante), Renan Santos (Missão) e Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) — Foto: Montagem/g1

Os candidatos à Presidência da República votaram na manhã deste domingo (4) e, em seguida, devem acompanhar a apuração dos votos ao longo do dia em seus estados.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) , Augusto Cury (Avante), Romeu Zema (Novo), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) e Renan Santos (Missão) já votaram.

O candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) foi o primeiro entre os presidenciáveis a votar neste domingo (4). Ele chegou às 8h, logo após a abertura dos portões ao lado da esposa, Fernanda Bolsonaro.

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) foi o próximo a votar. Ele chegou acompanhado da primeira-dama, Janja da Silva, e do candidato a vice-presidente em sua chapa, Geraldo Alckmin (PSB), em São Bernardo do Campo (SP).

O presidente estava acompanhado do vice Geraldo Alckmin, das candidatas Marina Silva e Simone Tebet e de Fernando Haddad.

Se vencer as eleições deste ano, Lula exercerá o quarto mandato no Palácio do Planalto e chegará a 16 anos como presidente. Ficará atrás somente de Getúlio Vargas, que governou o Brasil por pouco mais de 18 anos, mas que só foi eleito presidente pelo voto direto uma vez.

O presidente brasileiro e candidato à reeleição pelo Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT), Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, segura a bandeira nacional ao lado do vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin, ao chegar para votar nas eleições gerais em São Bernardo do Campo, Brasil, em 4 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Amanda Perobelli

“Hoje é um dia glorioso para o país. Uma página virada. Estou confiante na vitória e certo de que temos participação em nível nacional. Estou certo de que podemos ganhar as eleições”, afirmou.

Na sequência, o presidente criticou a venda de armas e a atuação de milicianos. “O Brasil não vai para a frente com venda de armas, mas com distribuição de livros. Não vai para a frente com milicianos, com orgia em torno do Banco Master, vai com o caráter dos seus governantes”.

O candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) votou na manhã deste domingo (4), no Rio de Janeiro. Ele chegou às 8h, logo depois da abertura dos portões da Escola Municipal Barão Homem de Mello, em Vila Isabel, na Zona Norte.

O candidato disse estar preparado para presidir o país e afirmou que pretende devolver às famílias brasileiras, segundo ele, o direito de voltar a sonhar.

“É um dia muito importante, onde eu espero que o brasileiro ponha fim a essa era do atraso que apostou tudo, que vale tudo. Que perdeu a linha de usar dinheiro público, a máquina pública, para tentar interferir nas eleições. Os amigos do Lula interferiram nas eleições e isso tem que mudar. O Brasil não aguenta mais quatro anos disso”, disse o candidato ao deixar a zona eleitoral.

Candidato Flávio Bolsonaro vota na Zona Norte do Rio — Foto: Reprodução

Segundo colocado nas pesquisas de intenção de voto, Flávio Bolsonaro é o representante do bolsonarismo na disputa presidencial de 2026.

Aos 45 anos, o senador pelo Rio de Janeiro é o filho mais velho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL) e foi escolhido como candidato do partido no fim de 2025, após disputas internas.

O candidato à presidência Augusto Cury (Avante) votou na manhã deste domingo (4) na Escola Municipal de Educação Fundamental (EMEF) Coronel José Venâncio Dias, em Colina (SP).

Antes do voto, ele disse à imprensa que as propostas dele são robustas e inteligentes.

Augusto Cury vota em Colina, no interior de São Paulo — Foto: Reprodução/Globonews

"Todos que leram meus projetos, todos economistas, todas as pessoas, todos empresários, gestores, disseram que nunca viram um projeto tão robusto, tão inteligente, não apenas para os 4 anos, mas para os 25 anos. Talvez seja o projeto mais robusto, mais inteligente da história de um candidato à Presidência".

O candidato à presidência Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) votou na manhã deste domingo (4) no Colégio Estadual Zizi Perillo Caiado, no Setor Central, em Nova Crixás, no norte goiano.

Ronaldo Caiado, de 77 anos, tenta conquistar o cargo pela segunda vez, após ter concorrido em 1989. Oficializou sua candidatura à Presidência em julho, anunciando como vice Gilberto Kassab, presidente nacional do PSD.

Caiado vota neste domingo em Nova Crixás (GO). — Foto: Divulgação

O candidato à presidência Romeu Zema (Novo) votou na manhã deste domingo (4) na Escola Estadual Delfim Moreira, no Centro de Araxá.

Ele chegou ao local por volta das 9h e foi acompanhado por apoiadores. Em um vídeo registrado do candidato na cabine de votação, é possível vê-lo olhando para o celular enquanto vota.

Segundo o Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de Minas Gerais (TRE-MG), violar o sigilo do voto é crime previsto no Código Eleitoral. Porém, para haver punição, é necessária uma denúncia formal feita pelo Ministério Público.

romeu zema vota com celular na mão em araxá — Foto: Caio Ranieri/TV Integração

Em entrevista à imprensa, Zema disse que não foi impedido de utilizar o aparelho na seção.

"Eu ando com o celular o dia todo, né? Ele é quase como se fosse um dedo. Ninguém me lembrou ali e eu fui votar normalmente, mas isso não afetou em nada o meu voto, a minha forma de votar. Não fotografei nada, não fiz nada com o celular ali. Fui só votar mesmo. A colinha estava no papel, levei no papel".

Romeu também afirmou estar confiante na candidatura e disse esperar que eleitores em todos os estados reconheçam sua trajetória como gestor nos setores privado e público.

“Certeza, nós vamos mostrar que temos eleitores em todos os estados do Brasil, em todas as cidades, pessoas que ainda acreditam numa proposta de mudança de alguém que tem histórico de gestão tanto no setor privado quanto no público”, afirmou.

O candidato à presidência pelo Missão, Renan Santos, votou na manhã deste domingo (4) em uma escola estadual da Zona Sul de São Paulo.

A partir das 17h, o candidato acompanhará a apuração de votos na sede do partido, na capital paulista, em um evento fechado à imprensa.

Após a apuração, ele deve participar de uma coletiva de imprensa na região do Morumbi, também na Zona Sul.

Renan Santos vota em São Paulo. — Foto: Carlos Henrique Dias/g1

articles.title: TRE-SP registra troca de 118 urnas até as 11h; votação segue sem prejuízo aos votos, diz presidente | G1
articles.standfirst: O número representa 0,102% das 114.605 urnas utilizadas na votação em São Paulo. Presidente do TRE pede que eleitores levem 'colinha' para votar.
articles.summary: O número representa 0,102% das 114.605 urnas utilizadas na votação em São Paulo. Presidente do TRE pede que eleitores levem 'colinha' para votar.
articles.body:
TRE-SP faz balanço de urnas trocadas — Foto: Reprodução

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de São Paulo (TRE-SP) informou que 118 urnas eletrônicas precisaram ser substituídas em todo o estado até as 11h deste domingo (4), primeiro turno das eleições de 2026. O número representa 0,102% das 114.605 urnas utilizadas na votação em São Paulo.

Segundo o presidente do TRE-SP, desembargador Encinas Manfré, o número de substituições é considerado pequeno e as ocorrências não provocaram prejuízo aos votos já registrados pelos eleitores.

Das 118 urnas substituídas, 27 estavam na capital paulista, o equivalente a 0,093% das 28.922 urnas da cidade. Outras 91 foram trocadas no interior, ou 0,106% das 85.683 urnas utilizadas fora da capital.

Entre os municípios que tiveram substituições estão Campinas, com quatro urnas; Guarulhos e Jundiaí, com três cada; e Americana, Barretos, Franca, Iguape, Itupeva e Mauá, entre outras cidades.

Durante a primeira entrevista coletiva do dia, realizada às 11h, Manfré também comentou os problemas provocados pelo temporal em Presidente Prudente, no interior paulista. Um local de votação teve o telhado atingido pela chuva.

Segundo o presidente do TRE-SP, a situação já foi superada e não haverá comprometimento da votação no município.

Manfré também comentou relatos de demora para votar e reforçou a orientação para que os eleitores levem uma “colinha” com os números dos candidatos.

Segundo o presidente do tribunal, eleitores que chegam à urna sem lembrar os números dos candidatos acabam levando mais tempo para concluir o voto, o que prejudica o fluxo das seções e pode contribuir para a formação de filas.

A recomendação é que o eleitor deixe anotados previamente os números dos candidatos em quem pretende votar para agilizar o processo dentro da cabine.

O TRE-SP também realizou neste domingo testes de autenticidade em urnas de dez seções eleitorais do estado. Os equipamentos foram selecionados no sábado (3), em cerimônia pública, e passaram por uma verificação para confirmar que os sistemas instalados são os mesmos que foram abertos, compilados, assinados e lacrados pela Justiça Eleitoral antes da eleição.

Em uma das verificações, realizada em uma escola municipal na Zona Norte da capital, foram examinados o extrato de carga da urna, a mídia de resultado e as assinaturas e os resumos digitais dos arquivos. Segundo o TRE-SP, todas as verificações ocorreram normalmente.

Além dos testes de autenticidade, 33 urnas passam pelo Teste de Integridade neste domingo. O procedimento ocorre simultaneamente à votação oficial, em ambiente monitorado por câmeras, e compara votos previamente registrados em cédulas de papel com aqueles digitados nas urnas eletrônicas.

Os procedimentos fazem parte das auditorias realizadas pela Justiça Eleitoral no dia da votação. Os chamados resumos digitais, ou hashes, permitem verificar se os arquivos encontrados nas urnas correspondem aos sistemas que foram lacrados pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) para a eleição.

articles.title: Ken Paxton’s estranged wife urges voters to back his Senate bid, yet avoids mentioning him by name
articles.summary: The estranged wife of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton urged voters to stand behind the entire Republican midterm ticket in an ad released Saturday, though she neglected to name Paxton directly.
articles.body: The estranged wife of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton urged voters to stand behind the entire Republican midterm ticket in an ad released Saturday, though she neglected to name Paxton directly. Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton, who filed for divorce from Paxton last year citing “biblical grounds,” appeared in an ad telling Texans that she is “voting for the Republican ticket on Nov. 3,” but did not cite Paxton’s Senate bid by name. She did, however, invite voters to “talk about the elephant in the room.” “In a general election, it’s not as much about the individual players on the team; it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line,” Paxton said in the ad. “Either we hold every Republican seat, or we hand the future of Texas to the other team.” Angela Paxton’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether she plans to vote for her estranged husband herself. Ken Paxton’s tenure as attorney general has been beset by allegations of abuse of office and bribery. Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives in 2023, but the state Senate later acquitted him. The Senate trial, however, touched on allegations of infidelity. Paxton has denied any wrongdoing. The ad comes as Paxton’s daughter, Mattie Hayworth, recently appeared in an ad for her father alongside her husband and children. Hayworth criticized “liberal politicians” as a graphic showing Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., alongside Paxton’s Democratic opponent, James Talarico, came over the screen. “When they come after you, my dad goes after them to bring down prices and stand up for families,” Hayworth said. As Election Day nears, Talarico holds a slight edge over Paxton, defying the deep-red profile of Texas, where Republicans haven’t lost a statewide race since 1994 and Democrats haven’t won a U.S. Senate seat since 1988. According to an NBC5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll in late September, Talarico was at 46% and Paxton at 43%, within the survey’s margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The poll acknowledges another 8% of potential voters who are still undecided in the race. NBC News currently defines the race as a toss-up. The ad featuring Angela Paxton, which was funded by Texas PAC, a political action committee affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, comes as the Texas Senate race has become one of the most expensive in the current cycle. President Donald Trump, who endorsed Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary, has urged voters to get behind the state attorney general. His super PAC, MAGA Inc., has also put millions into Paxton’s race. The president has visited Texas twice in the last month — first for the GOP midterm convention in Dallas and then again this week for a rally in Denton, which comes as part of Trump’s 17-state campaign blitz. In a separate campaign appearance Friday night in Alabama, Trump reiterated the high stakes associated with Texas’ race. “Last night, I went to Texas, where we won by a lot, and then I went to Oklahoma, and they said, ‘Why is he going to Texas?’” Trump said. “Because we have to win that race. Ken Paxton has to win.”

articles.title: Trump touts ‘golden age’ at Ohio rally, urges voters to deliver GOP midterm wins
articles.summary: President Donald Trump urged Ohio rally-goers to "pretend I'm on the ballot" as he stumped for Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy in the midterms.
articles.body: President Donald Trump swept into Ohio Saturday night promoting what he calls a new "golden age" for America, pointing to billions of dollars in investment and new jobs in the Buckeye State as he urged voters to help keep Republicans in power in November. For the third time in as many nights, Trump rallied supporters outside Dayton for Republicans Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, casting the midterms as a chance to extend the economic and political gains he said the GOP has delivered since his return to the White House. And with his own name absent from the ballot, Trump gave voters gathered a simple instruction. TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG "Just pretend that I’m running," Trump said. "When I run, we win." Trump, who carried Ohio in all three of his presidential campaigns, later echoed the same message as he sought to rally his political coalition behind Republicans fighting to maintain control of Congress. "If you don’t mind, please pretend that I’m on the ballot," Trump said. "And you need to turn out for a midterm victory." The president used much of the rally to make an economic case for the Republican ticket, declaring Ohio is "booming" as he hailed investments he credited to both his trade and tariff policies. Trump pointed to a $400 million Stellantis investment in Toledo and an $850 million Electra aerospace investment near Springfield. Weaving in an anecdote about his daily aspirin habit, the president also featured Bayer’s plans for a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing campus near Columbus, which the company says will support approximately 600 permanent jobs and 1,500 construction jobs. "Your state is booming," Trump told the gathered crowd. "Every state is booming." FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY Trump credited the investments to his tariff agenda, arguing the U.S. is finally leveling the playing field after years of other countries using tariffs against American products while giving companies a powerful incentive to build at home. The president also threw his support behind Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation aimed at shielding consumers from additional electricity costs associated with data centers. "We want them," Trump said of data centers. "There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China." Husted brought the legislation to the Senate floor days before the rally, where it failed to advance. President Trump pledged to sign it if Congress can send it to his desk. TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE' "I will sign this Ratepayer Protection Act into law immediately," Trump said. Trump broadened his victory lap from Ohio to the country as a whole, hailing stock market records, manufacturing growth, investment and employment while contrasting his own administration’s economic record with former President Joe Biden's. "Our nation is doing better now than ever before," Trump said. He also praised GOP-backed tax provisions, including no tax on tips and overtime, and reiterated his previously announced proposal for $5,000 payments to adult Americans if Republicans retain the House and Senate. Trump then shifted to immigration and Springfield, Ohio, dedicating his recitation of the poem "The Snake" to the city that became a national flashpoint during the 2024 presidential campaign over an influx of Haitian nationals into the community. "I dedicate this to Springfield, Ohio," Trump said. "They went through hell." After finishing the poem, which the president has long admired as an immigration allegory, he told the crowd, "That’s what happened at our border," before hailing his administration’s immigration crackdown. The president also briefly touched on Venezuela, claiming the U.S. had more than recouped the costs of its military operation against former Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro through the country's vast oil resources. "We paid for the cost of the war many, many times over," Trump said. "We’re making a fortune with it." Trump repeatedly weaved the election 31 days away into his remarks, urging Ohioans to support Husted, Ramaswamy and Republican congressional candidates. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He also pitched Ohio as a potential home for the U.S. National Space Academy, citing both the state's aviation history and the Wright brothers. "If we win the midterms, Ohio will be very, very strongly considered for this," Trump said. "I really want you to go out and vote again for John Husted and for Vivek."

articles.title: Trump, campaigning in Ohio, says the midterms will bring a ‘big surprise’
articles.summary: VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate.
articles.body: VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate. “I think we’re going to have a big surprise, because they don’t know what’s happening,” Trump said while speaking onstage inside a high school gymnasium near Dayton. “Just get out and vote,” Trump added. “If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big. And we’re going to shove it up their ass.” The visit, part of what White House officials have told NBC News will be a push through at least 17 states between now and Nov. 3, was aimed at boosting incumbent Sen. Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP nominee for governor. Trump, who won Ohio three times by comfortable margins, opened his speech with praise for both before moving into broader remarks to promote himself and his administration. He also offered support for local Rep. Mike Turner and for several House candidates in attendance, including Derek Merrin, the Republican running against longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur in northwest Ohio. Husted’s bid to keep the Senate seat — which he was appointed to after JD Vance was elected vice president — has in particular become a subject of concern among Republicans in Ohio and Washington. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that Husted’s past enthusiasm for building data centers was hurting his campaign. Others have expressed worries that Husted, who has long wanted to be governor, has not put his full heart into the race. The battle is one of the most expensive and competitive Senate races in the country this fall. Along with a handful of other key contests, the clash between Husted and Brown could determine partisan control of the chamber. This week, Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, poured another $14 million into Ohio to prop up Husted, bringing the group’s investment in the state to $93 million. “Senator Jon Husted votes to put Ohio first, and he votes all the time,” Trump said before relating conversations he’s had with Thune and others: “They think he’s phenomenal.” The high school gym where Trump spoke Saturday night was a smaller venue than has been typical for his rallies. The home court of the Butler High School Aviators seats up to 5,000. There were several stretches of empty seats in upper bleachers as Trump took the stage — and many more by the time he finished speaking 93 minutes later. In Ohio and elsewhere, Republicans are wrestling with how to win at a time when polls show Trump and the war in Iran are highly unpopular and when voters most loyal to Trump might stay home because he’s not on the ballot. “As a lifelong Republican who’s voted in every election since I was 18 and in every primary election as a Republican, I have real concerns that we’re going to be able to turn out the every-four-year Trump voter,” Nick Owens, a former GOP chair in Ohio’s Brown County and former member of the state Board of Education, told NBC News last month. “I have real concerns that those voters just will not come to the polls.” Trump acknowledged that dynamic explicitly Saturday and repeated an argument he’s been making on the campaign trail this fall. “When I run, we win,” Trump said. “But for some reason, when I don’t run, they draw 44% less people. So what I’m going to do is ask you to just pretend that I’m running, because if we do, and if you draw the people, you’re going to win, and we’re going to win big.” Husted, speaking to reporters before the rally, described Trump as a unique asset in his race. “Well, he won Ohio by 11 points in the last election, and if we get those same voters to turn out in this election, we’ll win,” Husted said. Alex Triantafilou, the Ohio GOP chair, told NBC News that the rally was “hugely important” in the effort to motivate those low-propensity, Trump-loyal voters. “We know in Ohio that if we turn out the same electorate that we turned out in 2024, that we’ll win every race,” Triantafilou said in an interview. “Nobody speaks to that crowd better than President Trump.” The Saturday rally included a cameo from Jon Gruden, the former NFL coach who years ago was a teammate of Husted’s on the University of Dayton football team. “Jon Husted is a lot more than my friend,” an animated Gruden told the audience. “He was a great player. … He will never quit on you or anybody.” Trump marveled about Husted’s football-playing days, of which he said he was unaware until hearing about them from Gruden. “Nobody told me you were a great athlete,” Trump said, before taking a jab at his Democratic rival: “And Brown was not — he was not an athlete. That guy can’t tie his shoes.” For its part Saturday, the Brown team sent a mobile billboard linking Husted’s support for the war in Iran to higher gas prices through Dayton and on the streets near the rally. “Jon Husted has turned his back on working families — he’s only looking out for his billionaire buddies and special interests,” Brown said in a statement from his campaign. Ohio also is home to what polls show is a close race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. Ramaswamy faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician who served as the state’s health director under DeWine. Ohioans have not elected a Democrat as governor in 20 years, but at a time when high prices rate as a top-of-mind concern for voters, there are questions about the billionaire Ramaswamy’s appeal, especially in the rural parts of the state. Ramaswamy, like Husted, addressed the crowd early during the rally, and Trump invited both to return to the stage during his speech for additional remarks. Trump introduced Ramaswamy by noting how he had briefly run against him for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination. “He was a nasty guy,” Trump said of Ramaswamy. “But you know what? He was smart. He loves the state. He’s actually got a great heart.” Compared with Husted, Ramaswamy was otherwise less of a focus of Trump’s remarks. Trump, for example, criticized Senate Democrats who this week blocked Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to rein in higher utility costs associated with power-hungry data centers. Republicans, Trump said, are “taking historic action to ensure that Big Tech data centers benefit local communities.” Trump then made the argument for data centers, despite the fears it could be a losing issue for Husted. “We want them,” Trump said. “Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China.” Trump also recited the lyrics to the 1968 Al Wilson song “The Snake” — a recurring, crowd-pleasing bit in his rally speeches — with a new, localized twist. Trump dedicated the song, which he uses as an allegory to trusting communities that welcome immigrants, to nearby Springfield, Ohio. The city became a flashpoint in the 2024 presidential election after Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating dogs and pets. At another point, the crowd broke into chants of “four more years” for the term-limited president. “I’d love to do the four-more-year thing,” Trump responded in a teasing tone before suggesting that the press would overplay his remarks. “We’re driving them totally crazy,” Trump said, referring to the media. “But I love doing it. I love being with you. I really do.”

articles.title: Trump backs data centers in Ohio amid tight Senate race
articles.summary: President Trump defended data centers at a midterm campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio Saturday, arguing that the U.S. will risk losing ground in the global artificial intelligence race against China without the massive facilities that have come under heightened scrutiny in recent years. “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just…
articles.body:
President Trump defended data centers at a midterm campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio Saturday, arguing that the U.S. will risk losing ground in the global artificial intelligence race against China without the massive facilities that have come under heightened scrutiny in recent years.

“There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump told the crowd at a rally in the Buckeye State, where data centers have emerged as a flashpoint in one of the country’s most competitive Senate races.

The president argued that the facilities, which provide the computing power needed to develop and run AI systems —which he has now dubbed “superintelligence” — would be a beneficial investment in Ohio.

He also promised that his administration is working to ensure data centers “benefit local communities.”

Opposition to new data centers has grown across the country, with residents and lawmakers raising concerns about their enormous electricity demands and water usage that could drive up utility bills for consumers.

Backlash over data centers has emerged as a pain point for Republicans ahead of the rapidly approaching midterm elections.

Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President Vance and is currently facing a competitive challenge from former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), has faced criticism over his support for bringing data centers to the state while serving as lieutenant governor.

Husted, who was at the Saturday rally, has introduced a bill that sought to address those concerns by requiring large power users to shoulder more of their costs. The GOP-controlled Senate tried to advance the legislation, but it was ultimately blocked by Senate Democrats.

Brown has sought to make the issue a liability for the Ohio Republican.

“Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio,” Brown wrote Friday on the social platform X . “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.”

Trump, however, has repeatedly backed the buildout of data centers while dismissing concerns about the rapidly growing and powerful technology as his administration pushes to expand AI infrastructure in the U.S. to compete with China.

articles.title: Aliança Catalana de Sílvia Orriols empataría a escaños con el PSC en Cataluña
articles.standfirst: Según la reciente encuesta de Ipsos para La Vanguardia
articles.summary: Según la reciente encuesta de Ipsos para La Vanguardia
articles.body: Aliança Catalana, de Sílvia Orriols, experimentaría un crecimiento meteórico en las próximas elecciones autonómicas de Cataluña, pasando de los dos escaños a los 30. Así lo plantea la última encuesta de Ipsos para La Vanguardia, realizada entre el 23 de septiembre y el 1 de octubre a 2.000 personas. Según estos resultados, la formación nacionalista empataría con el PSC, de Salvador Illa, formación que actualmente gobierna la Generalitat, que perdería 12 diputados (de 42 a 30). Esquerra Republicana de Cataluña (ERC) pasaría de los 20 escaños a los 23 y, en cuarto puesto, estaría VOX, con una subida notable: pasaría de 11 diputados a 18. El quinto partido político en Cataluña sería Junts, con un descenso enorme en sus resultados: de los 35 actuales, sumaría 16 en los siguientes comicios autonómicos. El Partido Popular (PP) también baja: de 15 bajaría a 11. La mayoría absoluta en Cataluña está cifrada en 68 escaños. Esto plantea un escenario muy complejo en la comunidad autónoma. En base a los resultados de la encuesta de Ipsos, ninguno de los partidos podría alcanzar esta cifra. A no ser que lo hiciera con pactos que, a día de hoy, parecen muy poco probables. La alianza entre PSC (30) y ERC (23), por ejemplo, sumaría 53 escaños. Necesitaría a Junts, lo que se antojaría como una sociedad bastante sorprendente actualmente. Sí existe, numéricamente, la opción de que Aliança Catalana (30), VOX (18), Junts (16) y PP (11) sumen para formar gobierno en la Generalitat. Aunque, de nuevo, se trata de una combinación, sobre el papel, difícil viendo las distintas posturas que defienden las formaciones en cuestiones como el nacionalismo catalán. En definitiva, la encuesta de Ipsos dibuja un escenario de delicada, y virtualmente imposible, gobernabilidad en la comunidad autónoma. Las elecciones en Cataluña podrían celebrarse el próximo 2028.

articles.title: Gonzalo Bernardos, tajante con Pedro Sánchez: "Ha hecho lo que más le conviene para continuar en Moncloa"
articles.standfirst: El economista pone en duda los últimos movimientos del Ejecutivo en materia de vivienda
articles.summary: El economista pone en duda los últimos movimientos del Ejecutivo en materia de vivienda
articles.body: El debate económico, político y social en España vuelve a situar el acceso a la vivienda en el centro de la polémica nacional. El conocido economista y profesor titular de la Universidad de Barcelona, Gonzalo Bernardos, ha arremetido con dureza a través de sus redes sociales contra las recientes medidas regulatorias en materia de alquiler impulsadas por el Gobierno de España, señalando de forma explícita la estrategia política trazada por el presidente del Ejecutivo, Pedro Sánchez. A través de una serie de publicaciones compartidas en su cuenta oficial de la red social X (anteriormente Twitter), Bernardos ha vertido severas críticas sobre las consecuencias negativas que, a su juicio, ocasiona la intervención directa de los precios de los inmuebles. El analista subraya de forma insistente la sólida formación académica del líder socialista para dar mayor solidez a sus argumentos: "Pedro Sánchez es economista y sabe los perjuicios que genera el control de alquileres", sostiene con rotundidad el docente catalán en uno de sus mensajes más comentados. Asimismo, el mediático profesor ha recordado diversas intervenciones públicas donde se contrapone la postura intervencionista actual de la administración con posicionamientos pasados del propio presidente respecto al mercado inmobiliario y la necesidad de mantener la seguridad jurídica. Para el experto, la adopción de topes a las rentas y decretos no responde a criterios técnicos ni a la efectividad real para facilitar el acceso a un hogar, sino a meros cálculos tácticos para la gobernabilidad. "¿Ha hecho lo contrario de lo que piensa? Probablemente, sí. No obstante, ha hecho lo que más le conviene para continuar en Moncloa", sentencia con firmeza el analista. El contundente pronunciamiento del economista no ha tardado en hacerse viral en las plataformas digitales, avivando de forma inmediata la discusión entre defensores de la regulación estatal y aquellos profesionales del sector inmobiliario que advierten sobre el inminente riesgo de contracción en la oferta de pisos y la creciente desconfianza generada entre los pequeños propietarios.

articles.title: How an Uzbek truck driver’s fatal crash exposed troubling fraud trend in Middle America: ‘Chameleon carriers’
articles.summary: Uzbek-linked trucking companies in southwest Ohio face scrutiny over CDL fraud, English proficiency violations and fatal semi-truck crashes on U.S. roads.
articles.body: CINCINNATI, OH - A young man killed by an Uzbek truck driver earlier this year in Ohio, along with several instances of illegal immigrant truck drivers involved in fatal crashes, has sparked a larger conversation in southwest Ohio about fraud, crime, immigration and how gaps in trucking industry oversight are putting Americans at risk. Tobias "Toby" Forsythe, a 21-year-old goalkeeper from Ohio on the University of Massachusetts Lowell men’s soccer team, was killed July 5 when authorities say a semi-truck driven by 42-year-old Uzbek national Bekhzod Asrarov, who entered the country under the Biden administration's diversity visa lottery program, rear-ended Forsythe’s Honda Accord on Interstate 71 in Madison County, Ohio. It was later determined, according to court documents, that Asrarov could not speak or understand English well enough to communicate with responding state troopers without the use of Google Translate, despite holding an Ohio commercial driver’s license, and that he allegedly removed a dashboard camera from his truck after the fatal crash in an effort to conceal or destroy evidence. "We cannot let truckers like Asrarov, who can’t read our road signs or speak to law enforcement, drive 80,000-pound rigs on America’s highways," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X after the crash. IMMIGRANT TRUCK DRIVER ADMITTED TO US UNDER BIDEN ALLEGEDLY KILLS UMASS SOCCER STAR, SPOKE NO ENGLISH In southwest Ohio, a researcher known as Nodawolf has been sounding the alarm to his growing follower count about a vast network of trucking companies, many of them owned or operated by Uzbek nationals, that have popped up in communities like Loveland, Middletown, and Maineville, where Asrarov resides, in recent years and could be contributing to the unsafe practices that took the life of Forsythe, and many others across the country. Nodawolf, who Fox News Digital granted anonymity due to the death threats he’s received from his online reporting, said his research has focused on what he describes as an interconnected network of Uzbek-linked trucking companies in southwest Ohio, including companies that have donated money toward construction of a local Islamic center, according to the center's own website. "All of them have English violations and have manipulated ELDs," Nodawolf said, referring to electronic logging devices that track a trucker’s driving hours and are intended to enforce federal limits on how long drivers can stay behind the wheel. The Islamic Center, located in Maineville, told Fox News Digital that a "charitable contribution or participation in a community fundraising activity, by itself, should not be interpreted as evidence of an ownership, employment, contractual, commercial, or other business relationship with the Islamic Center or its leadership." A Fox News Digital review identified hundreds of trucking companies and other trucking entities registered in Maineville and surrounding southwest Ohio communities, including dozens that were registered in recent years. A separate review of companies identified as connected to the local Uzbek community found serious FMCSA safety violations, including drivers cited for failing English-proficiency requirements and other federal trucking violations. TRUMP ADMIN TRUCKING CRACKDOWN LANDS 51 IMMIGRATION DETENTIONS, 36 ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY VIOLATIONS "This really concerns me, you know, as a father," Nodawolf told Fox News Digital. "I mean, it's clearly obvious that they either don't understand our laws, they don't care about our laws, or they know our laws and they're taking advantage of it." Nodawolf has reported on Uzbek trucking networks communicating on the social media platform Telegram. One of those Telegram channels, named "UzbegimAmerica," has routinely mentioned the Uzbek community in Maineville. Court documents show the owner of that channel, Farkhod Faiziev, is a suspected illegal immigrant from Uzbekistan. The Trump administration has made significant progress on the issue of removing foreign truck drivers who pose a danger being removed from the road – including a recent multi-agency operation in Arizona’s Yuma Sector, which led to the arrest of 95 illegal alien truck drivers earlier this month – striking at the heart of human and drug smuggling operations at the U.S. southern border. The Departments of Homeland Security, Transportation and Justice recently announced a coordinated crackdown on trucking and CDL fraud targeting fraudulent licensing, unauthorized employment, identity-document fraud, shell companies and other criminal activity. The effort includes inspections at more than 200 driving schools across 23 states, investigations based on more than 1,000 leads, enforcement operations targeting illegal immigrants with commercial licenses and a new multi-state DOJ task force focused on trucking-related fraud and roadway safety. A trucking-industry veteran with decades of experience who spoke to Fox News Digital under the condition of anonymity for his safety described a developing fraud scheme popular with immigrant communities known as "chameleon carriers", a network of trucking companies that appear separate on paper but, he said, share the same drivers, trucks and operations. The arrangement starts when operators establish one company that is "quote-unquote legitimate," he said, then create additional carriers and authorities while using the same underlying assets across them. ILLEGAL TRUCKER CASES FUEL GOP PUSH TO CRACK DOWN ON CDL MILLS AS DEMS LARGELY SILENT The point, the industry expert said, is to "spread out their safety liability across multiple companies." Rather than allowing inspections and violations to pile up under one carrier, he said, the operation can distribute them among multiple motor-carrier authorities. "If they have 10 inspections and 10 violations across 10 different companies, that doesn’t hurt the safety rating as much," he said. "But if it was one company that had 10 inspections and 10 violations, that one company is going to get hammered." The separate companies can also serve as a contingency plan, he said. If one carrier is shut down, loses insurance or becomes too damaged by safety problems, "they’re able to immediately move all of the equipment and drivers and everything under one of the different companies," the industry veteran said. "Their operation never stops. There’s no way to shut them down." He further alleged the structure can facilitate cargo theft, with a company disappearing after obtaining a high-value shipment while the broader network continues operating through its remaining entities. "They lost one of their shell companies, basically, but they just got $5 million in iPads," he said. The industry expert said the model can be particularly dangerous, in his view, because it allows companies to keep operating despite safety problems while allegedly using drivers who may not be legally authorized to work in the United States. He said operators can make that harder to detect by classifying drivers as independent contractors rather than employees, potentially avoiding the ordinary employee I-9 verification process. "If you’re using a bunch of people from a third-world country that just showed up in the United States as drivers, whether they’re here legally or not, how well do you think they’re going to maintain their equipment and be able to follow the laws?" he said. Seven of the trucking schools targeted by the Department of Transportation last month are located in Ohio, DOT told Fox News last month. A Notice of Proposed Removal was recently issued by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration for Turan CDL School, a Middletown-based company that has advertised CDL training to Uzbek speakers, including advertisements suggesting students could obtain a CDL without first learning English, as well as Google reviews from customers claiming they earned their licenses in as little as one week. ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’ "There's 'what do the rules say' and then 'what's happening on the ground," Andrew Poliakoff, vice president of the Commercial Vehicle Training Association, told Fox 28 Columbus shortly after the crash that killed Forsythe. "We're seeing now is that there are a lot of people committing fraud, and engaging in a variety of bad actions issuing commercial driver's licenses." Victor Louis, whose Cincinnati based company Load Secure verifies the identities of drivers entering its network, told Fox News Digital that he has seen local advertisements promising prospective truckers a CDL in as little as a week immediately raise red flags. "Trucking is such an inherently dangerous activity. Essentially, you're driving a 40-ton missile down the road," Louis said. "To think that someone is going to be certified to do that within a week, that may or may not speak English, like that doesn't make any sense." Louis said his company is also seeing a significant number of non-domiciled drivers, foreign drivers who hold commercial licenses issued by a U.S. state despite not having their permanent residence in that state. He said roughly 15% to 20% of drivers entering Load Secure's network fall into that category and estimated the figure could be around 20% among long-haul truckers nationwide. "Whether they're here legally or not, I don't know, but they are essentially foreign nationals," Louis said. He argued that long-haul trucking can be particularly attractive to migrants because drivers can spend weeks at a time living on the road rather than maintaining a permanent home near their workplace. Louis said cargo theft and the security of the broader supply chain are among his biggest concerns. "What we see with that market of non-domiciled drivers is a high propensity of cargo theft, an extremely high propensity," he said. "It’s wreaking havoc on our supply chain. Number one, it's extremely dangerous and number two, it is very unsecure. We don't know if things are being tampered with. This exposes our supply chains." The Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles told Fox News Digital that it is reviewing the state’s nondomiciled commercial driver’s license holders in coordination with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. Of the roughly 5,000 nondomiciled credentials originally issued, about 3,500 remain active, meaning approximately 1,500 are no longer active as the review continues. On Sept. 16, Fox News reported that ICE arrested two Uzbek illegal alien truck drivers in New Jersey as part of nationwide crackdown on fraudulent CDLs. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are starting to go into those thousand leads of fraud, waste and abuse into our trucking industry," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a press conference last month. "We're going to prioritize going after employees that are suspected of accepting payments to help illegals bypass driver's license and CDL requirements." In Brown County, Ohio, on Sept. 2, an Indian national with a CDL out of California crashed his semi-truck head-on into the car of 50-year-old Brenda Watson, who died at the scene. The driver, Manjit Singh , was later determined to be an illegal immigrant and ICE announced in a press release that a detainer was placed along with a charge of aggravated vehicular homicide. "One state’s regulatory failure becomes every state’s highway threat," Ohio attorney Mehek Cooke told News Digital. "Republican governors cannot assume their states were insulated from Biden’s border crisis simply because they opposed his policies." Fox News Digital reached out to Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine's office for comment. Last month, ICE launched a tip-line for reporting fraudulent CDL licenses. "Too many American lives have been lost or permanently changed because illegal aliens who have no business being on our roads have been granted CDLs," Mullin said in a press release. "ICE and our federal partners, including the Department of Transportation, will be cracking down on CDL fraud so that not one more American life is lost to a reckless illegal alien behind the wheel of a semi-truck."

articles.title: Cornell allegations fuel bipartisan push for stronger sexual assault protections
articles.summary: Lawmakers across the aisle are pushing for stronger protections for sexual violence survivors after a former Cornell University student’s fraternity house gang rape allegations drew national attention last week. While the woman first accused the seven men of raping her for several hours at a fraternity house in 2024, the reports sparked a nationwide controversy…
articles.body:
Lawmakers across the aisle are pushing for stronger protections for sexual violence survivors after a former Cornell University student’s fraternity house gang rape allegations drew national attention last week.

While the woman first accused the seven men of raping her for several hours at a fraternity house in 2024, the reports sparked a nationwide controversy in September after she filed a lawsuit against the university and other allegedly involved parties — putting renewed focus on efforts in Congress to address sexual misconduct.

Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) and Kat Cammack (R-Fla.), chairwomen of the Democratic and Republican Women’s Caucuses, respectively, launched a bipartisan effort earlier this year to take on the issue within the Capitol. The effort came in response to several male lawmakers facing accusations of domestic abuse and dating violence, as well as inappropriate sexual contact and harassment toward female staffers.

The Cornell case is adding new urgency to those efforts , as lawmakers confront questions over whether existing policies adequately protect survivors and hold institutions accountable.

“The allegations at Cornell are deeply disturbing, and we need to make sure students are protected and perpetrators are held accountable. There are actions that can be taken at both the state and federal levels, including greater oversight and stronger protections for students,” Rep. Nicole Malliotakis (R-N.Y.) told The Hill in a statement.

“New York State should revise its current law to address the ‘voluntary intoxication’ loophole and instead consider the totality of the evidence, including cases where a victim is too intoxicated to consent. State and federal laws should complement each other to ensure victims have adequate protections. We should also ensure Title IX is being properly enforced and that institutions that repeatedly fail to investigate or report serious incidents are held accountable, including potentially putting federal funding at risk,” she added.

Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) wrote on the social platform X Friday that he is “deeply disgusted and angered” by the Cornell allegations.

“Sexual assault is a crime, not a campus disciplinary matter. New York should require allegations to be immediately referred to qualified law enforcement for an independent investigation, with a special prosecutor when appropriate,” Lawler wrote. “Universities have a responsibility to protect their students and enforce their own codes of conduct, but they should not be the ones determining whether a potential crime occurred. Any of our daughters could be Jane Doe, and they deserve better. We need to make sure that anyone who commits sexual violence, and anyone who knowingly enables or conceals it, is held accountable.”

Cammack’s office declined to comment for the story.

This past week, the Education Department announced it had formally rescinded the Biden-era Title IX interpretation that gave sex-based discrimination protections to students on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Schools must now go back to the Title IX code as held under the previous Trump administration in 2020, a pivot the department said will protect women’s sports. But critics have argued the move would only weaken protections for sexual assault victims.

Democrats, in particular, have bashed the Trump administration’s rollback of Title IX protections. Rep. Deborah Ross (D-N.C.), policy task force co-chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, told The Hill that the Trump administration “has now made it harder for victims of sexual assault on college campuses to get justice” with its adjustment to sex-based discrimination law.

She continued, “That is no surprise because they have been cutting education funding, cutting sexual assault and domestic violence funding and really doing a disservice to people who are victims for this entire administration.”

“But I think that is where we need to shine the biggest light because this happened on a college campus. And if those new Title IX regs went into effect, and if the funding for Title IX enforcement went into effect, and if allowing dual prosecutions was continuing, that would give a remedy to sexual assault survivors.”

The Democratic Women’s Caucus in January released its first “Women’s Safety Legislative Slate,” a package of bills aiming to create new support programs for sexual violence survivors and gender-based violence prevention initiatives, among other matters.

Ross also highlighted a bill she introduced alongside Reps. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) and Leger Fernández, dubbed the Survivors’ Rights Restitution Act. The legislation would “create a restitution fund in the judicial branch for survivors of sexual violence whose rights were violated by the federal government,” according to a Sept. 15 press release.

“Believe me, we are taking this seriously, and I think the whole situation with the Epstein survivors is something that has brought the nation’s attention to this issue in a bipartisan way,” Ross said.

Leger Fernández told The Hill in a statement that the Democratic Women’s Caucus “has been sounding the alarm on the pervasive culture of sexual violence for years.”

“We stand with Jane Doe and hope her case is a turning point for Republicans in Congress. Women’s safety in workplaces, the military, and college campuses are under threat; the least Republicans can do is condemn what took place at Cornell and work with us to enact stronger and more robust Title IX protections for student survivors,” Leger Fernández continued.

When asked by NBC whether he thinks Cornell has done enough to investigate the alleged rape, President Trump said, “I don’t know that much about it, but Cornell’s a fine school. I’m sure they’ll do what’s right.”

Trump also criticized the Thursday appointment of New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) as a special prosecutor investigating the Ivy League school’s rape case, arguing that “whoever she’s looking at … won’t get a fair shake.”

Along with its chair, another Republican Women’s Caucus member, Rep. Julie Fedorchak (N.D.), held off on commenting on the Cornell Controversy — her office telling The Hill they will “wait to comment as there is an ongoing and active investigation.”

Still, Ross said she expects some of the sexual assault prevention bills introduced by her colleagues to garner bipartisan support and is looking to the lame-duck period for opportunities to advance those efforts.

“Between now and when we come back after the election, we will have to see which bills may get a hearing and could move forward, and which bills we might want to try to do a discharge petition on, and which bills will just be part of our slate and our agenda for the next Congress,” Ross said.

Lexi Lonas Cochran and Julia Manchester contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump funnels millions from massive war chest into key House, Senate races: Here’s where
articles.summary: President Trump’s super PAC and affiliates have injected tens of millions of dollars into pivotal Senate and House races just one month from Election Day as the GOP looks to keep control of Congress. Trump’s MAGA Inc. and several affiliated groups — No Going Back PAC Inc. and Safety & Affordability PAC Inc. — have reported some of their…
articles.body:
President Trump’s super PAC and affiliates have injected tens of millions of dollars into pivotal Senate and House races just one month from Election Day as the GOP looks to keep control of Congress.

Trump’s MAGA Inc. and several affiliated groups — No Going Back PAC Inc. and Safety & Affordability PAC Inc. — have reported some of their biggest spending so far in the toss-up Ohio, Texas and Michigan Senate races. They have also spent heavily in a slew of competitive House races in states like Florida, New York, Michigan and Maine.

Political observers and candidates alike are keeping a close eye on Trump’s immense war chest and where he will spend next. As of late August, MAGA Inc. had $415 million on hand, and the president has pledged to spend between $400 million and $500 million in the midterms.

One Republican operative involved in the midterms noted that if things go south for the GOP in the fall, it’ll be primarily because voters say costs of living are still too high, not a lack of money spent.

Here’s a look at where Trump’s super PAC and affiliated groups are spending:

The president’s main super PAC has funneled most of its resources into the bitter Texas Senate race between state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) and state Rep. James Talarico (D). It has reported spending $25 million so far on the toss up race, according to the latest campaign finance filing available Saturday .

A polling average of Texas Senate surveys compiled by Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) shows Talarico edging Paxton out by more than 2 percentage points.

In late August, Trump’s super PAC also reported spending just more than $825,000 to support Sen. Darline Graham (R) in the South Carolina Senate GOP primary against Rep. Ralph Norman (R). Graham ultimately won the primary to face Democrat Annie Andrews for the full six-year term.

These figures don’t include future ad reservations.

Republicans have worried about who will foot the bill in Texas in particular. Paxton has been mired in controversy after surviving an impeachment trial, and the Senate Republican campaign arm opposed his candidacy in the nasty GOP primary against Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

However, Texas PAC, which is affiliated with Senate GOP leadership, has already reported spending more than $130 million to boost the Texas attorney general and oppose Talarico, per its latest filing .

A source familiar with the Trump political operation’s spending suggested the difference in spending between Trump and Senate Republicans’ groups was “not a discrepancy,” adding “we’ve communicated to partners in the ecosystem what we were going to do.”

“Everything we’ve done has been in partnership” with Congressional Leadership Fund and the Senate Leadership Fund, the source familiar said, “looking for gaps or where we need to strategically make a dent” during certain time periods or certain media markets.

The Trump-affiliated super PAC is spending in a swath of competitive Senate and House races.

So far, it’s spent close to $23 million in the Ohio Senate race between Sen. Jon Husted (R) and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), according to a Wednesday filing. Another $17.5 million has been poured into the Michigan Senate race between former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

A separate nearly $10 million has been spent to boost former Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Michael Whatley and attack former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in North Carolina’s Senate contest.

Another $7.4 million has been spent in the New Hampshire Senate race between Rep. Chris Pappas (D) and former Sen. John E. Sununu (R), while more than $5 million has been spent to support Rep. Mike Collins (R) and oppose Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) in the Georgia Senate race.

No Going Back PAC has also spent more than $5 million in the Alaska Senate race.

Of that money raised, close to $43 million has been spent in aired advertising among those six Senate races, according to a Wednesday report from ad-tracking firm AdImpact . More than $32 million has also been spent on aired advertising for competitive House seats.

Nearly $26 million has been reserved for future ad buys in five of those six Senate races, according to the firm: Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Alaska and Georgia.

Republicans, overall, hold a clear advantage in spending this cycle, though that hasn’t stopped competitive Senate and House Democratic candidates from outraising their GOP counterparts.

AdImpact reported Thursday that this is the first time Republicans have held the Senate spending edge at this point of the election cycle since at least 2020, outspending Democrats by nearly $190 million.

No Going Back PAC is also heavily investing in House races.

The group has invested more than $7 million in Florida’s battleground 25th District, where Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D) and Republican Scott Singer are duking it out as well as close to $6.6 million in New York’s 3rd District represented by Rep. Tom Suozzi (D) and close to $4 million in Michigan’s 4th District represented by Rep. Bill Huizenga (R).

But it’s also notably spending in red districts amid a tough midterm environment for the GOP.

No Going Back PAC, for example, has spent about $285,000 in Texas’s 9th District that was redrawn last year to favor Republicans. Republican Alex Mealer is running against Democrat Leticia Gutierrez in a race that DDHQ rates likely Republican.

The group has also poured more than $235,000 in Texas’s 23rd District, which DDHQ also forecasts will remain in Republican control. Pro-gun YouTuber Brandon Herrera, who’s had a history of making controversial statements, is running against Democrat Katy Padilla Stout.

The source familiar with the Trump political operation’s spending said they’re looking to avoid allowing Democratic attacks to go unanswered in GOP districts, while challenging the party from expanding their map in a way that avoids forcing Republicans to prioritize where to commit resources. At the same time, the group is also focused on expanding Republicans’ own map in districts like New York’s 3 rd and 4 th Congressional Districts and Florida’s 14 and 25 th districts, as examples.

Other Republicans, however, are sounding the alarm over the super PAC’s spending in red states paired with Trump’s recent visits to reliably GOP areas.

Recent and upcoming visits to Nebraska, Oklahoma and Alaska are “warning signs that something’s not right or that there’s concern, because those aren’t rally points that you’re doing … unless you’re actively running for president,” said a GOP operative involved in a 2024 presidential super PAC.

A second Trump-aligned super PAC is also starting to play in several competitive congressional races.

It filed its first official spending report with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) Thursday, showing the group spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in toss-up House districts.

The PAC spent $250,000 to oppose Democrat Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania’s 7th District, just shy of $190,000 to oppose Democrat Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin’s 3rd District, and almost $845,000 against Democrat Amish Shah in Arizona’s 1st District. Brooks and Cooke are challenging GOP Reps. Ryan Mackenzie and Derrick Van Orden, respectively, while Shah is up against Republican Jay Feely for an open Scottsdale-area seat.

The GOP operative involved in the midterms said Democrats have particularly been effective in using health care issues like the expiration of Affordable Care Act (ACA) tax credits and the cuts to Medicaid as a result of Republicans’ mega-policy package last year as examples of cost-of-living issues.

Bloomberg Government reported that the group is also spending in Maine’s purple 2nd District, as well. CNBC reported last month that the group had reserved at least $27 million in ad reservations.

articles.title: Southern Baptist president calls on pastors to 'step up' ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: Willy Rice says pastors must "step up" on abortion, marriage, gender identity and immigration, arguing these political issues are deeply theological.
articles.body: Southern Baptist Convention President and Pastor Willy Rice called on pastors across the country to "step up" into the political process as midterm elections near. While some Christian leaders advise against wading into politics from the pulpit, Rice argues pastors have long played a key role in American politics. Members of the theological and political left have shown no hesitance to mix religion with their politics and evangelicals should not either, he says. DETROIT PASTOR SAYS PROGRESSIVE CANDIDATES ARE TRYING TO 'VIRTUE-SIGNAL' TO CHRISTIAN VOTERS "Should pastors engage in the political process? They absolutely should. Because there are many political issues that are, at their heart, theological issues and moral issues that strike at the very center of what we believe to be true and what we believe people need to know in order to flourish personally and as a culture." "I think the pastors need to step up. I think throughout American history, pastors have had a strong voice at key moments in American political history," Rice said. 'JESUS WAS A RADICAL': PROGRESSIVES INVOKE CHRIST TO SELL LEFT-WING AGENDA ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL Rice lamented that many Christians have been encouraged in recent decades, from both external and internal forces, to "be more quiet" and "withdraw from the political process." "Now, the interesting thing is that those on the theological and political left did not [withdraw], and they had no intention of doing so. And in fact, statistics show that people on the political and theological left are actually more politically engaged than those on the right," Rice said. "So what you had was, for a period of time, I felt like you had an almost a vacuum that kind of developed, a silence that was there with a lack of Christian leaders leaning in." PRO-LIFE GROUP RAMPS UP NC GROUND GAME AS REPORT FINDS FED ABORTION MESSAGE GIVES GOP CANDIDATE BIGGEST BOOST Rice highlighted abortion, the definition of marriage, gender identity and immigration as issues where Christians should feel compelled to vote in a certain way. articles.title: Real voters reveal what could decide the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: With Election Day about a month away, real voters talk with NewsNation about what issues matter to them most.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — With Election Day about a month away, voters from Texas and Alabama told NewsNation economic pressure, distrust of politicians, national security and even artificial intelligence are influencing how they view the 2026 midterm elections .

Texas independent voter Sandi Hebley said AI-generated political advertising has become a new concern as Republican Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a competitive Senate race.

“I’d rather hear from the actual people than something that some committee somewhere made up,” Hebley said.

The Texas contest is among the nation’s most competitive Senate races. Recent polling has shown Paxton and Talarico separated by only a few points, with some surveys giving Talarico a narrow advantage.

NewsNation reported Sept. 30 that both campaigns are also courting crucial Hispanic and Black voters.

NewsNation reported both campaigns are also courting crucial Hispanic and Black voters.

Democratic voter says party must ‘step up its game’ to unite voters

Democratic voter Andrea Cervantes said her party needs to rethink its message.

“I think that Democrats need to step up their game,” she told NewsNation, arguing that Democrats should focus less on progressive politics and more on the issues Americans face every day.

Cervantes also called for greater transparency and said neither party is immune from corruption. She warned that Democrats currently lack unity, pointing to the appeal of identifying as an independent among voters who do not feel firmly represented by either major party.

The economy emerged as common ground among the panelists. Gallup’s long-running Most Important Problem survey tracks Americans’ concerns about issues including the economy and government, along with which party voters believe can better address their top concern.

Hebley said rising costs are likely to follow voters into the voting booth.

“I think a lot of folks are struggling,” she said, citing the pressure of paying rent or a mortgage while also buying gas to get to work.

NewsNation has reported that inflation, housing and fuel costs remain significant political concerns.

From pocketbook pain to national security, voters weigh midterm stakes

Republican voter Ajua Mason acknowledged higher prices but argued that voters should consider national security alongside their finances. She defended President Donald Trump’s policies toward Iran, saying she is willing to accept short-term financial pain if the administration ultimately makes the country safer.

Those competing priorities could help determine control of Congress. As of Oct. 1, NewsNation election partner Decision Desk HQ gave Democrats a 75% chance of winning the House, while Democrats held a 54% chance of capturing the Senate, making control of both chambers highly competitive.

With voters preparing to make that choice, the panel illustrated why the outcome remains uncertain. Concerns ranged from AI-generated campaign material and distrust of political parties to grocery bills and foreign policy, underscoring how candidates are competing for voters whose priorities do not necessarily fall neatly along party lines.

articles.title: Congressional hearings are no longer a check on power — they’re now a circus
articles.summary: Unfortunately, despite a vast expansion of executive branch authority, Congress seems prepared to let partisan advantage trump comity, cooperation and the public’s right to know. And with Republicans now controlling Congress and the White House, reform seems out of reach.
articles.body:
Congressional hearings are supposed to educate the public and provide information that Congress needs to legislate effectively and hold the executive branch accountable.

Members of Congress have also used oversight hearings to generate publicity and criticize administration officials of the other party, while witnesses tout their policies and dodge difficult questions.

These days, oversight hearings have degenerated into partisan brawls. Confident they will not be disciplined by committee chairs from their own party, administration witnesses often launch personal attacks instead of answering legitimate questions.

Congress need not permit its hearings to turn into a circus. It has the power to control witnesses and compel testimony. But in today’s hyperpartisan environment, it lacks the will.

FBI Director Kash Patel’s recent appearance before the Senate Judiciary Committee offers one of many cases in point.

Chairman Charles Grassley (R-Iowa) opened the hearing by praising Patel’s leadership, accusing the Obama and Biden administrations of conducting “secret, insidious, and downright evil operations,” and warning Patel that Democrats would “personally attack you, [and] question your ethics, your truthfulness and your abilities.”

Ranking Democrat Dick Durbin (Ill.) promptly blasted Patel as “the least qualified and most partisan FBI director in our nation’s history.”

Several hours of acrimony followed. When Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) asked Patel reasonable, albeit partisan, questions about election integrity, Patel accused him of “lying about the men and women of the FBI.” Asked to pledge not to interfere with voting in the midterms, Patel called the question a “charade of lies,” accused Welch of staging a “campaign ad” and demanded to know why the senator’s wealth had supposedly “increased 4,000 percent” since he entered the upper chamber.

Patel’s barbs weren’t spontaneous. A Reuters’ photograph showed him holding typed bullet point attacks on at least one committee Democrat.

Appalled by the failure to answer many questions, Democrats responded with what was often, though not always, justifiable outrage. Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), for example, accused Patel of “stonewalling” and called him a “thug,” an “incompetent lackey,” “an embarrassment to the agency,” “a disgrace,” and “a mockery.” Patel shot back, “you are the biggest mockery in the United States Senate.”

Offensive questions and comments from some committee members, however, do not obviate administration officials’ obligation to provide Congress with the information it needs to fulfill its legislative and oversight responsibilities. But instead of directing Patel to respond appropriately to legitimate questions, Grassley let the hearing run its course.

Evasive testimony and partisan indulgence by committee chairs are not new. During the Biden administration, former Attorney General Merrick Garland, for example, repeatedly evaded questions from Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) about whether he had sought an ethics opinion concerning his son-in-law. Instead of directing Garland to answer, Durbin, then committee chair, told Cruz his time had expired .

But there is a profound difference between evading hostile questions and launching irrelevant personal attacks on the elected officials asking them.

During her October 2025 testimony to the Senate Judiciary Committee, Attorney General Pam Bondi repeatedly ducked questions on everything from the Epstein files to the decision to prosecute former FBI director James Comey. Instead, she accused Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) of lying about his military record, Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) of supporting antifa, and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) of accepting inappropriate campaign contributions.

Like Patel, Bondi came prepared with dirt on committee Democrats. Tellingly, administration officials shared clips of Bondi’s insults in real time on social media.

At a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February, according to The Washington Post, Bondi arrived “ armed with scripted insults for Democrats .” When ranking Democrat Jamie Raskin (Md.) objected to her deliberately using up Democrats’ allotted question time, she called him a “ washed-up loser lawyer .”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr ., and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem have been similarly combative.

The hostility comes as Congress hears from administration officials of either party less and less often.

The Senate Foreign Relations Committee held only 24 hearings and briefings with Biden administration witnesses in 2021; last year, it held two full committee hearings with Trump administration witnesses. Administration appearances before the House Foreign Affairs Committee fell from 47 to 12. This year, Trump administration officials are stonewalling Congress on the war in Iran.

Congress bears some responsibility for this problem. Members deliver speeches disguised as questions, trade insults with witnesses, and grandstand for social media. Committee chairs tolerate evasive and insulting responses, despite repeated complaints from members of the other party. Under Trump, committee chairs appear to treat alignment with the administration as far more important than safeguarding Congress’s institutional prerogatives and responsibilities.

Congress could claw back some of its authority if committee chairs were prepared to subpoena those who refuse to testify, direct witnesses to answer pertinent questions, and pursue contempt proceedings against uncooperative witnesses.

Unfortunately, despite a vast expansion of executive branch authority, Congress seems prepared to let partisan advantage trump comity, cooperation and the public’s right to know. And with Republicans now controlling Congress and the White House, reform seems out of reach.

If Democrats regain control of one or both houses of Congress in the midterms, they may well rein in administration witnesses. Otherwise, oversight hearings will offer only political theater, “full of sound and fury , signifying nothing.”

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.
