articles.title: GOP Senate candidate's estranged wife confirms who she's voting for amid divorce proceedings
articles.summary: Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton urges voters to back the GOP ticket without naming estranged husband Ken Paxton, who faces James Talarico in a tight Texas Senate race.
articles.body: Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton is addressing the "elephant in the room," saying she’ll vote Republican this November without mentioning one GOP candidate by name: her estranged husband, Ken Paxton. Angela Paxton, who filed for divorce from the Texas Republican Senate candidate last year on "biblical grounds," says in a new political ad that she will back the Republican ticket on Nov. 3, arguing that keeping the seat in GOP hands outweighs concerns about any individual candidate. "People have asked my thoughts about this election, and turns out, I have some," she says in the ad. "Let’s talk about the elephant in the room." GOP FORTRESS IS UNDER THREAT IN ONE KEY RED STATE, AND THESE VOTERS COULD DECIDE WHETHER IT FALLS "In a general election, it’s not as much about the individual players on the team; it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line," she continues. "Either we hold every Republican seat, or we hand the future of Texas to the other team." "That’s why I’m voting for the Republican ticket on Nov. 3," she adds. "Let’s hold the line together." The ad does not mention Ken Paxton by name, but its message comes as the Republican Senate candidate faces a tight general election contest against Democrat James Talarico. The latest Fox News Poll, released Thursday, found Talarico with 51% support among Texas likely voters and Paxton with 49%, a difference within the poll’s margin of sampling error. The same poll found 50% of likely voters preferred Republican control of the U.S. Senate, compared with 49% who preferred Democratic control. Angela Paxton has previously signaled that maintaining Republican control of the seat takes precedence over her feelings about the individual candidate. During an address to the Texas Federation of Republican Women in September, she similarly framed the issue as the "elephant in the room" and told the audience that "it’s not the people, it’s the seat." REPUBLICAN CAVALRY ARRIVES FOR KEN PAXTON AS BIG-BUCKS TEXAS OFFENSIVE OPENS CASH FLOODGATES "We have more control over that seat and the future when we control the seat, when it’s still in the family, even if we’re mad at them," she said at the time, drawing laughter from the audience. "If we lose it to the other team, the nuances that we want to fix with maybe a certain candidate are nothing compared to what it’s going to take to get it back," she added. GEORGE W BUSH RAISES MONEY FOR REPUBLICANS, BUT NOT KEY SENATE CANDIDATE Angela Paxton filed for divorce from her husband in July 2025 after 38 years of marriage. In the filing, she alleged that Ken Paxton had "committed adultery" and said their marriage had "become insupportable because of discord or conflict of personalities." She separately announced the divorce on social media, saying she had filed "on biblical grounds." "I believe marriage is a sacred covenant and I have earnestly pursued reconciliation," she wrote. "But in light of recent discoveries, I do not believe that it honors God or is loving to myself, my children, or Ken to remain in the marriage." The new ad was funded by Texas PAC, a political action committee affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune. articles.title: Trump vows GOP midterm victory: ‘We’re going to shove it up their a–‘
articles.summary: President Trump on Saturday pressed his supporters to go to the polls for next month’s midterms, promising a “big” GOP victory if they do so. “You got to get out and vote. You got to get out. You got to vote for these guys,” Trump told a crowd of supporters at a rally in Ohio…
articles.body:
President Trump on Saturday pressed his supporters to go to the polls for next month’s midterms, promising a “big” GOP victory if they do so.

“You got to get out and vote. You got to get out. You got to vote for these guys,” Trump told a crowd of supporters at a rally in Ohio on Saturday.

“Just get out and vote. If you do that, we’re gonna win and we’re gonna win big and we’re gonna shove it up their a–,” the president added.

Republicans are facing a challenging road ahead politically as the midterms approach . Trump’s approval rating is down, the unpopular war in Iran has hit the seven-month mark, Democrats have been outperforming the GOP in recent polling and Americans have expressed concerns about the economy.

According to Decision Desk HQ , Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 38.5 percent on Sunday morning, while his disapproval rating was at 59.1 percent.

Fresh polling showing Democrats doing well in Senate battlegrounds and states that may lean more right has created optimism that the party could take both chambers of Congress in the midterms.

In a recent Quinnipiac University poll, 51 percent of registered voter respondents said that if Election Day was that day, they wanted Democrats to lock down the majority in the House, with 39 percent saying they wanted Republicans to capture the lower chamber.

The Quinnipiac poll also found that 62 percent of respondents said they are against Trump’s handling of the economy and that 62 percent were against his handling of foreign policy.

articles.title: Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans
articles.summary: Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House.
articles.body: Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations. Like the broader electorate, Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living. There are clear signs his party is paying the price. A greater share of Latino voters hold negative views of the Republican Party than at any time since 2016, and Democrats have leads on issues like dealing with the economy, immigration, the cost of living, corruption and healthcare. Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question. Against that backdrop, Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%. That’s double the lead they had among Latino voters at this point in 2024, though not quite at the heights the party enjoyed at this time in 2018, according to NBC News polling from just before that election. Nearly a fifth of Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they do not prefer a Republican-controlled Congress, with 14% saying they support Democrats and 8% unsure in their preference. The shifts come after the Republican Party made Trump’s 2024 gains among Latino voters central to its plans to keep the House majority. In Florida and Texas, the party drew new, heavily Latino districts that looked deep red by the 2024 results — but many are shaping up to be competitive in the midterms as Latino voters’ preferences have changed. Statewide races in Texas, Nevada and more will also be shaped by the evolving Latino vote, though it will not move as one bloc everywhere in the country. The poll results, collected Sept. 21-28, “indicate a striking reversal of Republican gains with Latino voters and point to trouble ahead for Republican candidates in the midterms,” said Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the poll with Republican pollster Micah Roberts and his firm, Public Opinion Strategies. Latino voters comprised around a tenth of the total vote in recent midterm elections. Roberts referred to Latino voters as “the swingiest of swing groups,” calling the reversal since 2024 “stunning.” “What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier,” he said, adding: “Trump is a central figure. He’s had real consequences on our politics, and without his presence, I think none of these changes would be evident in the data among Latinos.” But the results among Latino voters are not all good news for Democrats, who have not seen their party’s image improve in two years. And while Democrats have a midterm lead, Republicans are pulling more Latino support than in any NBC News poll before the 2024 election cycle, too, dating back to 2012. “Despite a more favorable environment for Democrats, any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats,” Arroyo-Cardona said. Trump struggles Latino voters overwhelmingly disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living (78%), the economy (74%), foreign policy (68%) and immigration (69%). Trump’s best issue of the five tested is border security — where 39% approve and 58% disapprove of his handling. His marks on foreign policy, the economy and cost of living are significantly lower than where then-President Joe Biden sat with Latino voters in September 2022, when Democrats had a better-than-expected midterm result despite losing control of the House. Then, 60% disapproved of Biden’s handling of the cost of living and 54% disapproved of his handling of the economy. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of Latino voters say the president’s policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say his policies have helped and 11% who say they haven’t made much of a difference. Among Latino independents, just 10% believe his policies have helped the economy, while 72% believe his policies have hurt it. Meanwhile, inflation and the cost of living ranked as the most important issue to 33% of Latino voters. That made it the top issue in the survey — and a majority (52%) ranked it as the most or second-most important issue. Latino voters who say the cost of living is the most important issue also prefer a Democratic Congress by 22 points. That’s a shift from the 2024 poll, when Republicans had a 4-point edge among these voters. A sizable majority of Latinos (63%) say their family’s income is falling behind the cost of living, while 25% say it is staying even and 11% say it is going up faster than the cost of living, similar to findings in 2024. Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who participated in the survey, told NBC News in a subsequent interview that she voted for Trump in 2024 after a lifetime of voting for Democrats and convinced many of her friends to do the same. She was frustrated with the Democrats on the economy and on transgender issues. “It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake,” she said, calling Trump a “disappointment.” “I’m more embarrassed than my friends because I was the one who convinced them to vote for him,” she added. Santiago lambasted the president’s deportation policies as “brutal” and “cold,” while also saying the difficult economic climate is weighing heavily on her and her family. While immigration didn’t rank as highly on the priority list, Latino voters expressed similar frustration with Trump’s hard-edged deportation policies. Two-thirds say Trump’s immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, 22% say he’s struck the right approach, and 9% say he hasn’t gone far enough. While 83% support deporting all undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, just 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the U.S. Roberts, the Republican pollster, pointed to the difference between support for deporting serious criminals and deporting everyone in America illegally as he imagined “what might have been” for Republicans. “There is support for a certain level of immigration enforcement, but the Latino electorate believes it’s gone way too far,” he added. In the poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years. Eighteen percent say they or someone close to them has considered leaving the U.S. over the last two years over concerns about ICE enforcement, and 17% say they or someone close to them has considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE. Maria, a Florida voter in her 20s who responded to the poll, told NBC News in a follow-up interview that Trump has “fallen short” in the two years since she voted for him. She declined to share her last name while discussing politics. She highlighted frustration on the economy and on deportations, arguing that while Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst, “I’ve had many friends, family members deported.” “They were supposed to be here. They had paperwork, and it didn’t matter. And now they can never come back. One of my friend’s grandpas didn’t even get deported to his home country. He got deported to Mexico instead of Cuba,” she later added. Midterms fallout The numbers for Trump and Republicans could spell trouble in November in states and districts with sizable Latino populations. “In a lot of the heavily Hispanic and Latino districts across the country that Trump and Republicans did well, and better than ever in, in 2024, you’re going to see that reversal,” said Roberts, the Republican pollster, noting Trump’s tough numbers on immigration and the cost of living. “This entire poll is full of very clear directional signals that Latinos have turned from 2024 and are ready to make a different choice with regard to who’s in control of Congress,” Roberts said. Democrats’ 24-point lead on the generic congressional ballot is twice as large as their margin in the 2024 version of the poll. But it’s not nearly as wide as the 43-point lead the party enjoyed at this point in the 2018 midterms. Latino voters also now say Democrats would better handle the cost of living and the economy by significant margins, erasing the advantages Trump and Republicans have enjoyed in past elections. Latino voters favor Democrats to handle other issues, and they break even on which party would better handle border security. More voters also say Democrats are more likely than Republicans to share their values and address the concerns of the Hispanic community. Amid the economic frustrations, voters are also more motivated to head to the polls in November. A sizable majority (72%) rank themselves a 10 out of 10 in terms of interest in November’s elections, compared with 54% at this time in 2024. Meanwhile, 62% say they are more motivated to vote this year than in midterms past. And a majority (54%) say their midterm vote is meant to send a signal of opposition to Trump, while 21% say they want to signal their support for Trump and 23% say their vote is not about sending a signal to the president either way. While the poll results offer plenty of short-term upside for Democrats, they also outline longer-term changes trending against the party. While Latino voters’ negative views of the GOP have jumped since 2024, views of the Democratic Party have not improved. Now, 62% of Latino voters have negative views of the Republican Party, a 16-point increase from two years ago, while 42% have a negative view of the Democratic Party, a 4-point increase from 2024. “I’m still wary about the Democratic Party because I don’t really know that much other than what I was fed,” said Maria, the Florida voter in her 20s, before adding that she’s still leaning toward voting for Democrats: “I feel like I have to put my faith in them now to fix things.” She said she voted for Trump in 2024 in large part because her family instilled a fear of socialism and Democrats in her. The poll found that socialism remains underwater with Latino voters — 13% feel positively about it and 41% view socialism negatively, with 38 feeling neutral about socialism. Cardona-Arroyo, the Democratic pollster, noted that the party has work to do after the midterms to develop a broader message. “What do Democrats do to move beyond this place where they’re running on opposition to the Republican Party, which I think will work in ’26,” Cardona-Arroyo said. “It’s sort of an open question of whether that will work in ’28.” The NBC News/Telemundo poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters Sept. 21-28 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text messages. Overall, 20% of the interviews were conducted in Spanish. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

articles.title: How the shooting death of a Houston father is igniting Latino politics in Texas
articles.summary: HOUSTON — As the sun set on a late-September evening, a voice rose over the din of traffic at the roadside memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the 52-year-old husband and father fatally shot here by immigration authorities three months ago.
articles.body: HOUSTON — As the sun set on a late-September evening, a voice rose over the din of traffic at the roadside memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the 52-year-old husband and father fatally shot here by immigration authorities three months ago. Sitting on barbershop steps, Berta Lopez, a nearby resident, alternately sang, recited prayers and cried for a man she never met. “It was unjust — he was killed unjustly! The family is deeply hurt, his wife, his children. They are like family to us. And why don’t they show the people who did the killing? Why don’t they show them? Why don’t they release the names of the people who killed Lorenzo? Why don’t they expose them?” she said in Spanish. In tears, Lopez said that after more than a year of intensive operations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Salgado Araujo’s killing was a clarifying moment. The government, she said, saw those who weren’t U.S. citizens as less than nothing. She was tired of it. “Just because we’re Hispanic, shouldn’t we hold our heads high? No, God doesn’t want us hanging our heads in shame. He wants all of us, his children, to hold our heads up high,” Lopez said. “God doesn’t care about papers.” Lopez’s hurt and anger was reflected in NBC News interviews with more than three dozen Houston-area Latinos, elected officials, activists and political strategists. They reveal a distraught community whose members feel degraded by the messages they hear out of Washington, D.C., during President Donald Trump’s second term. They said they have been terrorized by the constant stories of those detained, many wrongly, and left to languish. They were aghast that the government was sending immigrants to countries they had never heard of. Many said Salgado Araujo’s shooting death crystallized their feelings of powerlessness. Most Latinos were better versed in the details of the incident than in the names and backgrounds of those running for some of the highest-profile offices in their state. Their refrains were in the same vein: That could have been my dad, my brother, my uncle, my son — or me. “They’re being unfair. They’ve lied about a lot of things. They’re killing innocent people, breaking families apart. It’s just not right. They have no sympathy for other people,” said Julio Roa, a Houston resident who lamented what he was seeing happen in his state. “I come from Mexican parents. I’m born a U.S. citizen, but I live it day by day when they’re scared to go to the corner store.” It all illustrates a political environment in which Republicans and Trump are bleeding support from Latinos. A new NBC News/Telemundo survey of 800 registered Latino voters nationally showed that fully 69% disapproved of the job Trump was doing as president, and 54% said they intended their midterm vote to be a signal of opposition to the president. The survey, carried out Sept. 21-28, had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Notably, immigration and border security did not score high among priorities in the survey, with 6% of Latino voters calling it a top issue. But it has hit a nerve: 67% of potential Latino voters said Trump’s immigration enforcement had gone too far. In an earlier NBC5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll of Texas Latinos, respondents ranked immigration and border questions as the second highest priority behind economic factors. That survey showed a sizable swing. In 2024, 55% of Texas Latinos supported Trump, according to exit polls, but recent surveys show statewide Democrats garnering at least 55% of the Latino vote. That’s part of the reason Texas’ Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton has become a battleground contest and why Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, is facing perhaps his toughest-ever general election challenge, from Democrat Gina Hinojosa. One man who once held a deep allegiance to Trump said he could not explain the regret he felt. “I’m guilty as charged. I voted for Trump. But I never thought it was gonna happen the way that this happened,” said Albert Riseño, a plumber who works in the Houston area. Riseño is a three-time Trump voter. He described a fear that has settled over the Latino community since Trump’s second term in office. “There’s no words to describe what’s going on,” he said. “Everybody’s scared.” Pushing back Lorenzo Salgado Araujo woke before dawn on a hot Houston morning on July 7, as he did most days. He had lived in the U.S. for decades without legal status but was in the process of getting a work permit. He had no criminal record. He picked up workers in his white van and was driving to a jobsite when he was pursued by immigration agents in unmarked vehicles. An officer shot him, according to authorities, after they say he used his vehicle to ram them. It’s a story contradicted by witnesses in the van, but it’s one immigration authorities have told before in explaining how a traffic pursuit turned deadly. This time, though, the family wasn’t having it. Salgado Araujo’s eldest son stood before cameras and delivered an emotional testimonial to his father that went viral. “He was a hardworking family man who never wanted his name to be known by anyone outside of his family,” Ronaldo Salgado said at a news conference days after his father’s shooting, as his brother held up a photo of their father. Ronaldo Salgado stressed that the story of his dad ramming government vehicles could not be true. Their father had always taught his kids that if law enforcement attempted to pull them over, they were to pull off the road, hand over their license and registration and act respectfully. In the end, authorities admitted Salgado Araujo was not the intended target of the operation. In an interview with NBC News, Ronaldo Salgado said as immigration arrests became more prevalent in 2025, they talked to their father about the procedure if he had an encounter, including calling his family, and that they’d contact their attorneys. “Just remember, don’t sign anything. Call us,” Ronaldo Salgado said he told his father. Sitting at Las Perras Cafe in Houston, where a makeshift altar to his father sits in the corner, Ronaldo Salgado recited the names of those who had been killed by immigration officers, including Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Ruben Ray Martinez, saying the country is not now safe because of their deaths. “These are lives that are lost, and they need to be investigated, just like any other life lost. It needs to be investigated with the full cooperation of the agents involved and the agencies involved,” the son said. “All of this isn’t making us any safer. How is going after my dad going to work making the city safer?” Ronaldo Salgado said. “Criminals don’t wake up at 5 in the morning to pick up their crew and go to do a day of backbreaking labor. You don’t.” In an unusual move, federal officials made public an FBI search warrant to get inside Salgado Araujo’s van after his death. Then, federal officials released a stinging detail: The bureau sought entry to look at baggies with crystals that they said resembled meth. When he heard that, Ronaldo Salgado said he couldn’t help but break into a little smile: “Ohhh, they messed up.” He knew what it was. And it would only make things worse for federal authorities. It was a homemade electrolyte mixture, mainly of salt, that his father later mixed into Gatorade for himself and workers to combat the triple-digit Houston summer heat outside. The U.S. attorney’s office later confirmed that the mix was in fact not methamphetamine, surprising few who knew Salgado Araujo. Ronaldo Salgado felt it was an effort to sully his father’s reputation and dampen public outrage. The implication just added to community anger, viewed as a thinly veiled attempt at smearing the man immigration authorities killed. “It really shook the community,” said Jasmine Khadem González, an immigrant rights organizer with the Houston Democratic Socialists of America. “A lot of us who are Latino, we have somebody in our family: If it’s not our father then it’s our uncle who has a very similar job. … To see somebody like that be targeted for just being on his way to work or for the color of his skin or for the kind of truck that he’s driving — because it’s associated with Latino men — to see somebody like that be targeted for doing a very everyday thing. For just existing.” In the NBC News/Telemundo poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years. Amy Zachmeyer, the executive director of New Economy for Working Houston, a group that helped organize community vigils and demanded accountability and transparency in the probe, said the Salgado family’s high-profile pushback kept authorities in check. “They’ve shown incredible strength to be able to really defend their father,” she said. Zachmeyer grew emotional as she spoke about the sons. “They never let a narrative set in that he was anything but a loving father, a Houstonian, a Texan, a hard worker.” Anger reshapes local politics Adrian Garcia, a Harris County commissioner, said Latinos are “feeling a lot of attack and disrespect.” Over the last year, he’s worked to reach out to those who don’t vote often. From his view, people now are willing to walk across broken glass to send a message to the Trump administration. “The low-propensity voters that I’ve been speaking to absolutely have a great intensity to vote in this election, and they specifically speak to ICE enforcement. A lot of young kids: ‘I’m voting for my mom. I’m voting for my dad.’ I hear that a lot,” Garcia said. More Latino registered voters than ever — 72% — rated their interest in the upcoming election as 10 out of 10 in the NBC News/Telemundo poll. Garcia described the greater impact that fear of immigration enforcement has had across the Texas economy. “This is not what our community deserves, and it is also what is impacting the things that we care about the most, the business, the economy. They’re hurting the industry,” he said. “They’re hurting those who work hard and play by the rules.” Jareli Barrera, who works as a server at the popular Cielito Cafe in Houston, said she has never been so tuned into an election. Today, she said she’s helping others, including co-workers, to register to vote. She cannot stand seeing the level of fear in her community, including among those who are citizens but fear being separated from family or an aggressive encounter. “Republicans are probably going to lose. It’s not going to be the greatest thing for them at the end of the day,” Barrera said. “Most of these immigrants are the ones that are making the U.S. successful. They’re doing the hard work. … If everyone’s deported, who’s gonna do the hard labor? Who’s gonna construct? Who’s going to do all this cleaning that they don’t want to do.” Since 2025, local activist groups have tried to work with the city of Houston to better protect Latinos as they watched intense enforcement operations in cities like Minneapolis, Los Angeles and Chicago upend life for residents and lead to encounters with immigration authorities that turned violent or deadly. Jennefer Canales-Pelaez, a Houston-based senior policy attorney and strategist with the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, said Salgado Araujo’s death was a “culmination of years of Texas entrenching itself, entangling itself with ICE” and “illustrated to them the fear, the levels of persecution of justice that immigrant communities have been living with in Texas for a very long time.” Before Salgado Araujo’s death, Canales-Pelaez was among those who worked to deter cooperation between Houston police and federal police agencies and pushed for greater transparency into immigration operations. Abbott, the three-term governor and a staunch Trump ally who is up for re-election in November, threatened to block $200 million in grants to Houston and other major cities if they didn’t change local rules that directed police forces not to hold individuals they encounter for longer time periods to assist ICE. The cities, including Houston, reworded their ordinances. Houston Mayor John Whitmire, a centrist Democrat, told The New York Times last October that he kept his head down as other city and state leaders in the country grew combative with the White House over immigration operations. Whitmire said his city had avoided “turmoil” that others faced. Whitmire initially declared his hands were tied after the shooting; the Houston Police Department had no jurisdiction to conduct an independent investigation. After community uproar, the city changed course. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare has now launched a probe, with the county government approving the $2.5 million request to fund it. “It ignited this flame and really showed other people that aren’t necessarily living this experience or working in this line of work, ‘Oh, this got to us,’” Canales-Pelaez said. “When the mayor told us that we weren’t going to be another Minneapolis, we weren’t going to be a Los Angeles, well, now we are. Someone’s dead. That really has sparked this rage, this collective, righteous anger.” Republican recalibration Abbott, who has long taken a hard-line stance on immigration, was silent on the Salgado Araujo shooting for a week but then ended up backing an independent investigation. “Immigration laws can be enforced, and stopping illegal immigration from coming across our border can be achieved, without shooting people,” Abbott said in mid-July. Paxton, the Republican state attorney general locked in a tight race with Talarico for the Senate seat, met with the U.S. Hispanic Business Council last week and made supportive statements about an immigration program designed to help industries in need of workers. Paxton has aggressively supported Trump’s immigration policies and in June boasted that his office had blocked public money to help pay for legal representation for immigrants facing deportation. Paxton had described the practice as “evil and wicked.” Last week, Paxton had a softer tone on another aspect of immigration. “Our birth population isn’t keeping up with demand, and so as long as we are doing this by the rule of law,” Paxton said, “I’m open to having help.” Ronaldo Salgado doesn’t rail against Republicans or Trump. He has stressed that the quest to investigate exactly what went wrong in a deadly encounter with law enforcement “should not be a partisan issue.” He also said those incensed by what they see should vote in November. “Immigrants’ rights shouldn’t be a partisan issue, and I just urge faithfully to look for and to vote for candidates who honor and respect the lives and rights of immigrants,” he said. “Every single elected official right now has immigrants living in their districts, in their states, their neighborhoods, and it’s their job to protect them. And if they’re not willing to protect them, then people should elect someone else that will.”

articles.title: Starship’s successful launch to low Earth orbit is a big deal
articles.summary: As the late, great science fiction writer Robert Heinlein said, “Once you get to Earth orbit, you’re halfway to anywhere in the solar system.”
articles.body:
Test 14 of the SpaceX Starship concluded recently with several milestones achieved that are important not only for the Artemis program but for the long-term fortunes of the company.

For the first time, the Starship achieved low Earth orbit. The feat was important for SpaceX’s goals of establishing a transportation system for the moon and Mars since, as the late, great science fiction writer Robert Heinlein said, “Once you get to Earth orbit, you’re halfway to anywhere in the solar system.”

The Starship also deployed 26 operational Starlink satellites, an accomplishment that established the launch vehicle as a money-making asset and not just as an experimental rocket.

It is unknown what the test cost, since the Super Heavy and the Starship were not recovered. But one estimate for a commercial Starship launch pegged the figure at $90 million. PJ Media suggested that the 26 V3 Starlink satellites deployed will generate $2.6 billion to $3.9 billion in revenue over a five-year lifespan.

Some glitches occurred along the way, however, which shows that SpaceX has some work to do before Starship becomes a fully functional operational spacecraft.

First, one of the Super Heavy’s engines failed. It was still able to deploy the Starship successfully and then splash down in the Gulf, but with a harder landing than SpaceX engineers would have liked.

Then, two of the Starship engines failed, causing the SpaceX ground crew to initially decide to abort the orbital insertion. However, ground controllers subsequently decided to burn the remaining engines longer and thus send the enormous spacecraft into its first orbital flight.

However, the SpaceX engineers decided to cut the mission short from 10 hours to about three and splashdown the Starship early. Call it another incomplete success.

SpaceX still has a lot to do before Starship becomes the operational spacecraft that will open up the moon, Mars and beyond to human exploration. The first thing that needs to happen is for SpaceX engineers to discover why the engines on the Super Heavy and the Starship itself failed and to develop a solution so that all of them run reliably every time.

The Starship has to prove that it can maintain an orbit, not just for a few hours, but for at least several days. It has to prove that it can maneuver while in orbit. Both capabilities are necessary before the Artemis III mission that will test rendezvous and docking between the Starship and the Orion spacecraft. The mission will also feature a rendezvous and docking between the Orion and the Blue Origin Blue Moon.

SpaceX has to transition from splashing down the Super Heavy and the Starship in the ocean to catching them both with the “ chopsticks ” back at the launch pad to facilitate reusability

To prove the Starship’s capability for moon and Mars missions, SpaceX must demonstrate that it can be refueled in low Earth orbit. The refueling effort will involve the launch of multiple Starships configured as tankers and their rendezvous and docking with the original vehicle bound for deep space.

Finally, before Artemis IV, the first crewed moon landing since Apollo 17 in 1972, can happen, Starship must show that it can land on the moon and, just as importantly, take off from the lunar surface.

To accomplish all of these things, SpaceX must increase the launch cadence for Starship. Test 14 took place about two months after the 13th test. The time between Starship launches must be compressed to at least weeks if the schedules for Artemis III and Artemis IV are to be met.

Still, in the midst of all the troubles besetting the world, with wars and rumors of additional wars abroad and political rancor at home, something remarkable is taking place at Starbase’s Boca Chica site, at the very southern tip of Texas.

When Apollo 17 departed from the moon, astronaut Gene Cernan said , “As we leave the Moon at Taurus-Littrow, we leave as we came and, God willing, as we shall return: with peace and hope for all mankind.”

Cernan did not live to see Artemis IV fulfill his vow. Who would have thought that the crucial man for the return to the moon would be a nerdy, eccentric immigrant from South Africa who was not even two years old when human beings last walked on the moon?

Thus, history is made by unlikely people and events.

Mark R. Whittington, who writes frequently about space policy, has published a political study of space exploration entitled “ Why is It So Hard to Go Back to the Moon? ” as well as “ The Moon, Mars and Beyond ” and, most recently, “ Why is America Going Back to the Moon? ” He blogs at Curmudgeons Corner.

articles.title: More Canadians to observe permanent daylight saving time. Why can’t the US?
articles.summary: For many across Canada, the clocks will not “fall back” an hour in November.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – More Canadians will not set their clocks back in November as they instead start to observe permanent daylight saving time, a move more than a dozen U.S. states stand ready to make but cannot .

Spurred by a survey of nearly 72,000, Manitoba officials announced in mid-September that daylight saving time is now permanent in the province.

“We heard from Manitobans loud and clear – no more changing the clocks in Manitoba,” Premier Wab Kinew said in a press release . Of surveyed residents, 92% wanted to see an end to seasonal time change, with 58% indicating they prefer permanent daylight saving.

A report by the Manitoba Health, Seniors and Long-Term Care department determined that getting rid of the twice-a-year clock change “would be better for population health than maintaining the status quo,” an argument some health officials in the U.S. agree with (though they support permanent standard time ).

On Sept. 23, officials in the Northwest Territories made a similar announcement , saying that over 87% of the more than 3,500 residents surveyed wanted to stop changing the clocks. Permanent daylight saving time was most commonly preferred.

In March, when daylight saving time began, British Columbia announced it was the final time it would change its clocks. Officials there suggested “recent actions from the U.S.” sparked the decision to make daylight saving time permanent. Alberta followed suit over the summer.

Yukon and most of Saskatchewan abandoned the twice-annual changing of the clocks in recent years.

Nineteen U.S. states , including five that share a border with Canada, have enacted legislation calling for their clocks to lock on permanent daylight saving time. It has yet to happen for any of them, however.

States can opt into year-round permanent standard time , as Hawaii and much of Arizona have done , but they need action by Congress to observe permanent daylight saving time. Legislation has been introduced in the House to allow states to lock their clocks on year-round daylight saving time, but the chamber won’t be back in session until November .

Outlook dim for daylight saving time bill in Senate

The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act earlier this year, and President Donald Trump has expressed his support for the bill. It would make daylight saving time permanent throughout the U.S., except for states like Hawaii and Arizona that opt for permanent standard time.

However, it seems unlikely that the bill will pass through the Senate anytime soon.

Wednesday night, the Senate adjourned for the midterm election . Senators are not scheduled to return to the Capitol until the week of Nov. 9. That not only leaves several key priorities in limbo but also likely means our clocks will be falling back as usual in a few weeks.

Daylight saving time ends on the earliest possible date this year , Nov. 1. That’s roughly a week before lawmakers are set to return, meaning the Sunshine Protection Act likely won’t be enacted in time to skip the seasonal time change.

The legislation faced an uncertain future in the Senate even before the chamber adjourned, but it’s possible that lawmakers pick the bill back up when they return.

In the meantime, our clocks will “fall back” to standard time on Nov. 1, the earliest possible date daylight saving time can end.

articles.title: Rahm Emanuel says Democrats should focus on ethics reforms rather than impeaching Trump
articles.summary: Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel said Democratic lawmakers should pursure ethics reforms rather than impeaching President Donald Trump if they win back the House.
articles.body: Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel called on Democratic lawmakers Sunday to set aside plans to impeach President Donald Trump if they win a majority in the House, pushing them instead to pass an ethics reform package. Asked directly on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” whether Democrats should take up impeachment in January if they take the House gavel, Emanuel said: “Short answer: No, because it’s not going anywhere, and it’s going to be a food fight, and it’s just going to be we return to the politics of fighting.” Emanuel, who served as President Barack Obama’s first chief of staff, proposed that Democrats could instead “pass an ethics package” to address the corruption he said is taking place in the Trump administration. In a September NBC News poll, government corruption emerged as the second-highest-rated issue voters were concerned about ahead of November’s midterm elections. On the airwaves, tackling government corruption and banning congressional stock trading has been a top issue in campaign ads from Democrats and Republicans. Should Democrats take back the House, Emanuel said, they should “hold [the Trump administration] accountable, and then pass an ethics package.” “You’re never going to get an impeachment,” he added. “Then if you do that, you just basically prove all Washington is what the American people think. It’s Disneyland on the Potomac. Deliver the change. Deliver a comprehensive ethics package that uses the investigations to then deliver change.” In September, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who could be speaker of the House if Democrats win a majority in Congress’ lower chamber in November, said his party’s top priorities would be to tackle healthcare costs and affordability. Jeffries has refrained from weighing in on calls from some fellow Democrats that the party should impeach the president if they take control of the House. In a June interview with “Meet the Press,” Jeffries told moderator Kristen Welker when asked about a potential impeachment: “We haven’t ruled anything in or ruled anything out in terms of accountability. What we have said is that our focus is going to be to make life more affordable for the American people. We have to drive down the high cost of living.” Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., last month told “Meet the Press” that impeaching Trump was not a “taboo” topic. “Everybody on our side understands that impeachment is a critical tool in the toolbox for constitutional self-defense against a president acting like a king, an imperious, lawless, arrogant king,” the Maryland lawmaker said, adding later in the interview: “Impeachment is not a taboo with us. It’s not a fetish with us.” Trump was impeached twice in his first term but was never convicted. Emanuel, who was also a two-term mayor of Chicago, is widely speculated to be considering a run for president in 2028. The New York Times reported last month that he has been a crucial behind-the-scenes player in the 2026 midterms, helping his party recruit candidates and offering advice to party leaders and candidates. The 2028 contest for the Democratic presidential nomination is expected to yield a crowded field of candidates, with nearly a dozen Democratic governors and members of Congress also fueling speculation that they’ll run. Asked Sunday on “Meet the Press,” whether he’ll run for president in 2028, Emanuel demurred, outlining affordability and building a positive vision for the future as the two most important issues facing the next president. “We’ve had two presidents back to back who’ve actually tried to restore a past that’s not coming back. Let’s build a future that we — actually, every American and every community in America is part of,” Emanuel said. “To me, if I have what it takes to answer that, I’ll do it. If I don’t, I won’t. And it’s that simple a question,” he added.

articles.title: Trump announces ‘Super Intelligence Force’ led by DNI Jay Clayton
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday morning announced the creation of “Super IntelligenceForce” amid his push to keep the U.S. in the lead on artificial intelligence development after warnings from the technology’s researchers. The task force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, whom The Wall Street Journal reported is expected to be named…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday morning announced the creation of “Super Intelligence Force” amid his push to keep the U.S. in the lead on artificial intelligence development after warnings from the technology’s researchers.

The task force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, whom The Wall Street Journal reported is expected to be named Trump’s AI czar .

“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” the president wrote on Truth Social , adding that the group “will coordinate the Federal Government’s engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies.”

The other members of the force are Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, under secretary of Defense for research and engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor.

It’s unclear if the announcement doubles as Trump officially naming Clayton to the AI czar position the president created. He has already ruled out Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent for the role.

Trump has sought to rebrand AI as “ super intelligence .” He recently signed a pledge with tech executives that put the name in writing across the executive branch. Diplomats have also been ordered by the State Department to use the term. The moves have been part of his push to reclaim the narrative on AI as researchers say its development could threaten humanity.

The pledge lays out a series of voluntary commitments for AI developers, including a promise to build internal controls and detection capabilities. Trump said after the pledge was signed that he was considering forming a committee that can “watch over the whole entity.” It’s possible that the “Super Intelligence Force” will act as this committee.

The president and other top Republicans have spoken of the need to stay ahead of China on AI development. Trump said recently that Chinese President Xi Jinping appeared to like referring to artificial intelligence as “super intelligence” during his state visit to Washington.

Superintelligence is already defined in the technology space as a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all of humanity’s cognitive performance.

articles.title: Sen. John Kennedy says he’s considering running for president
articles.summary: Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said that he is considering running for president in 2028.
articles.body: Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that he is considering a run for president in 2028. Asked by moderator Kristen Welker whether he was thinking about running for president, Kennedy replied, “Yeah.” “My plans right now are to run for re-election, but as I’ve said before, if I don’t think I can be effective in the Senate anymore, I would consider it,” he said. A slew of politicians on both sides of the aisle have acknowledged that they are considering running for president in 2028 or have declined to rule out the possibility. None, though, have formally announced yet that they are running. Kennedy, too, said that he has not made a decision. “On my side of the aisle, if a bunch of goobers run, and I think they’re goobers and one of the goobers might win, and I think I could do a better job, I would consider running,” he said. “But right now, I’m running for re-election.” Kennedy is up for re-election in 2028. Vice President JD Vance is widely considered a likely presidential candidate in 2028. Kennedy, though, declined to talk about Vance when asked why voters should pick the senator over the vice president. “I’m not going to talk about another potential candidate,” he said. “I’m just not there yet.” He added that he thinks “it’ll be good for both parties to have a full field.” President Donald Trump has previously floated both Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as potential successors. In September, Rubio said he has “no plans at this time” to run for president. NBC News previously reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has talked about potentially running for president in 2028, which a Pentagon spokesperson denied. Separately, Vance told NBC News last week that it was “really obvious to me” that Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, was running for president in 2028. The 2028 presidential election will be the first time since 2012 in which Trump will not be the Republican nominee.
